title: 'India's Got Latent' Gambit? Behind Vantika Agrawal's double bronze at Chess Olympiad | Exclusive
text: Vantika Agarwal opens up on Chess Olympiad and more NEW DELHI: The 46th edition of the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan's Samarkand, like usual, had just one rest day, after Round 6. Consequently, India's Vantika Agrawal, who had beaten US chess legend Irina Krush in that sixth-round matchup on Board 3, ended up with three days away from the board anyway â the scheduled rest day, plus two more rounds where she was kept off the lineup by captain Swayams Mishra , against Germany and Kazakhstan. Too much chess prep over those first two days had left Vantika looking for an escape on the third. Samay Raina's popular show 'India's Got Latent' came to her rescue. She binge-watched the latest episodes on her third day off, then returned to the board the next day and clinched a win over Uzbekistan's Nilufarkhon Imomkuzieva in her Round 9 matchup. "Usually I don't watch that much, because you don't get the time. You prepare in the morning, then at night you're checking your opponent and discussing, then preparing again in the morning. By the afternoon you have a game, and you're tired. But this time, with the rest day plus two more days off, I had a lot of time, and I thought I'd practised so much chess already; let me relax a bit. So I watched some India's Got Latent episodes," she told TimesofIndia.com. Watch Harika Dronavalli Exclusive: Inside Grenke #chess win, viral no-handshake incident, and more Asked if she enjoyed it, there was no hesitation. "Yes, of course," she added. "I'd watched earlier episodes too, and then the new one there. It's nice. You just relax a bit." Vantika ended her campaign with a score of 6/8, five wins to her name, and an individual bronze medal in India women's bronze-clinching campaign. It's the quieter of India's two medal stories from this Olympiad, and arguably the more interesting one to hear told from the inside. "I think it was good," she said of the experience overall. "I mean, of course, last time I won double gold. So this time also, we went for the gold, and it wasn't like we planned. We lost at the start to Poland. It wasn't as smooth as last year. But I'm glad that we won a lot of games and had a comeback, and managed to end on the podium; after a setback, we were able to come back and keep going. I think that was really important." The one that got away If there's a single result Vantika would look back with some disappointment, it's the Round 10 draw against China that effectively ended India's gold-medal hopes. The 24-year-old lost her game to Lu Miaoyi on Board 3, with the team setting for a 2-2 draw. "I was especially very upset about my game against China," the International Master (IM) admitted. "I think I was playing quite well, and after 40 moves it was very drawish. There were a lot of ways to make a draw. But somehow I was playing for a win at that moment. I knew my position wasn't better, but I decided to play for a win. Because of that, I made some foolish decisions." Part of the problem, she explained, was not knowing the full picture elsewhere. "At that moment it wasn't clear that we were winning on the fourth board, or I would have just gone for a draw. I was not sure what was happening on that board, and I thought I would play for a win," she recalled. Vantika Agrawal (on right) during the game against China (Photo by Rafal Oleksiewicz for FIDE) "Except for my loss against China, I think it was pretty good. Before that, I was on 5.5 out of 6. I had almost won all my games. If not for that loss, I would have even got an individual gold on board. "I won against Krush. Then, after three days of rest, I won against an Uzbek player, also quite strong. So I think it was good, except one game I wasn't happy about." Shaking off a bad result, she said, came down to a fairly simple discipline as she added, "I think it was just to focus on the next game, and not really think about what had already happened." A team built for the challenges Vantika credited the dressing room, and Mishra specifically, for how the team absorbed the Poland loss and kept pushing. "They all were very nice. Humpy (Koneru) was playing so well on board, Divya (Deshmukh), Savitha (Shri). Everyone was playing well. I think it can be seen that, in the end, we all won individual medals on our board," she remarked. "We were kind of prepared for that, because last year also we lost to Poland and had that setback. So we were prepared that if something goes wrong, we will come together and fight as a team." Vantika Agrawal against US chess legend Irina Krush (FIDE Photo) That same candour extended to the one selection question hanging over the campaign, which was Vaishali Rameshbabu's dip in form, which saw her dropped for the final rounds. "She is so strong she won the Candidates and is now the World Championship challenger. If she was in her full form, we would have easily crushed everyone. Those little chances that other teams got, like Poland, I don't think they would have got â we'd be winning on all boards," Vantika said. Asked whether the team dwells on these swings and misses while they're actually happening, Vantika was clear that they deliberately don't. "I don't think we really think about that. Everyone tries to focus just on their own game, and our coach decides who plays, who doesn't, so that everything goes well. We don't think that much about these things," she added. "Last time we had crushed everyone. We were 7 on 7, winning every game, not giving anyone a chance. This time it wasn't the same, even though we went with our best team. So the difficult part was accepting that every time you can't win gold, you can't crush everyone. It happens. That acceptance. That was difficult." The IM looking to make a mark in elite circuit When she was asked why she had been less visible on the elite circuit, Vantika Agrawal, already an Arjuna Awardee, was quick to push back on the perception that hers had been a quiet year outside the Olympiad bubble. "I'm not invited to these top tournaments where the other girls, Humpy, Vaishali, Divya, are playing," she told this website. "But it's not that I'm not active. I'm playing a lot of open tournaments, and I'd say I'm more active than them. If you check my profile, I've played more games than any of them. It's just that I'm not playing in the tournaments everyone covers." "My rating is a bit low, and it's not easy to increase â even when I play very well, I gain maybe five or seven rating points. It's not easy to reach that level, and only once you reach it do you get invited to those tournaments," she further noted. Vantika Agrawal at Chess Olympiad (FIDE Photo) "This year I beat Song Yuxin; she played board two for China, in an open tournament. I beat Aditya Mittal too, who's over 2600 and hadn't lost a game all year before that â he just lost to me." There was a touch of frustration in how she recalled one particular near-miss for recognition. "In the Tata Steel Rapid and Blitz in January, I tied for first place in Blitz, tied with Carissa Yip. But nobody covered that. It's just not being covered," she added with some disappointment. Whatever the coverage gap, Vantika insists it hasn't dented her own sense of where she stands and what she is aiming for â a Grandmaster (GM) title. "I already feel confident, and I'm continuously working. It didn't change much after this Olympiad. I just want to focus on my goals and not think too much about all this," she added. "I'll continue playing more tournaments, trying to improve my skills and my level." "I think I'll be doing the same thing, playing these open tournaments and trying to increase my rating, and see how it pans out," she admitted. ALSO READ: âSometimes in chess, there are just these blind spotsâ: Nihal Sarin looks back at his Chess Olympiad loss to Uzbekistan | Exclusive Her studies, meanwhile, are largely settled. "I've completed my B.Com Honours. I was at SRCC College, Delhi University. After that, I've been focusing more on chess, because I had exams in December that clashed with tournaments I really wanted to play. Right now, I'm completely focused on chess, but I'll keep the option open; if I want, I'll do my Master's or an MBA." title: Apoorva Mukhija opens up about leaked kissing video with Amin Jaz, admits she was UNAWARE that camera was rolling : 'When the clip surfaced I cried at Heathrow airport'
text: Apoorva Mukhija, popularly known as The Rebel Kid, has broken her silence on the viral video of her kissing Amin Jaz. In her latest vlog, she shared that the footage was shot at a private party roughly a year ago, and the two were completely unaware that they were being filmed. She remembered getting the news midway through her journey from Turkey to New York, while waiting out a layover in London. As a flood of messages about the clip arrived, she became overwhelmed and burst into tears at Heathrow Airport. Apoorva Mukhija breaks her silence on viral video Neither Apoorva nor Amin knew a camera was rolling at the party, she said. "One of my videos from a year ago has gotten leaked. So this video was like a private moment between me and another guy. And we did not know that we were being recorded. This was at a private party," she said. The discovery left her stunned. "Aur ye video bohot purani hai. 1 saal purani hai aur ab aayi hai baahar (And this video is very old. It's about a year old and has surfaced now)," she said. When she reached London's Heathrow Airport, her phone was already flooded with people asking whether she had seen the clip. "My entire WhatsApp is filled with messages saying, 'Did you see this?'", Apoorva recalled. Watch Why Rebel Kid Apoorva Makhija Left India for New York and What She Plans to Do Next Apoorva Mukhija's parents watched the clip too Things got even harder for Apoorva when she learned that her parents had watched the clip too. "This is the first time my parents saw that video. They did not know I had a boyfriend. They had no clue," she said. Coming on top of her private video suddenly spreading online, the realisation left her deeply shaken. Recalling that moment, she said, "So I have lost my mind." Apoorva Mukhija recalls crying amid the crowds at Heathrow Sitting amid the crowds at Heathrow Airport, Apoorva said she struggled to process what had just happened. "I remember I sat at the Heathrow airport, and there were, I think, a million people at that airport. Aur main bas neeche baithke roye jaa rahi hu, roye jaa rahi hu (And I just sat there and kept crying and crying)," she recalled. title: Fame & social media are just maya: Ranveer Allahabadia
text: From building an audience on YouTube to becoming one of Indiaâs most recognisable digital creators, Ranveer Allahabadia has experienced the many contradictions of online fame. Earlier, social media itself was a career, but I feel it is slowly becoming more of a marketing tool, to market yourself and your brand,â he says. He also points to the growing volume of content competing for audiencesâ attention. âToday, the supply of content and creators has grown tremendously, but the demand from audiences has remained almost the same. That makes this a very interesting and challenging phase for anyone trying to build an identity on the internet.â âThe harsh truth about fame is that it is never permanentâ Having spent more than 11 years in social media and influencer marketing, Allahabadia says he has watched different phases of popularity emerge and fade. âThe harsh truth Iâve realised about fame is that it is never permanent or predictable. The experience, he adds, has taught him not to become overly attached to visibility. âBuilding fame is one part of the journey, but knowing how to navigate away from it when the time comes is equally important,â he says. text: Instagram | From Tanzania To Haryana, Faizel Is Winning Hearts On Indiaâs Got Latent A clip from Samay Rainaâs India's Got Latent Season 2 has sparked an unexpected debate online, this time over foreign students studying in India and whether government-funded scholarships should be seen as an investment in diplomacy or as taxpayer money that ought to be prioritised for Indian students. The debate began after an X user, Neha Patel, shared a post about a Tanzanian student who appeared on the comedy show. According to Patelâs account, the student said he receives financial support from the Indian government while studying in India. She claimed he also sends some of the money he receives to his mother in Tanzania. Watch Samay Rainaâs âHelp Meâ Post Goes Viral After AI Video With Ranveer Allahbadia Breaks The Internet Her reaction was immediate: âBRO WHAT THE F**K?â Patel questioned why Indian taxpayers should fund stipends for foreign students when many Indian students themselves struggle to find seats, accommodation and other basic resources. âIndian students are struggling for seats, hostels and books,â she wrote, adding that she didn't want her tax money to effectively become a remittance sent to another country. âIâm not paying income tax so my hard earned money can become a family remittance to Tanzania,â Patel wrote. She also rejected the argument that such programmes should automatically be viewed as an act of goodwill. In her view, India should first focus on expanding educational infrastructure for its own students before spending public money on international scholarship programmes. The comparison quickly moved to Indiaâs higher education crunch. Patel cited figures around the number of students competing for IIT seats and the shortage of hostel accommodation at Delhi University, arguing that the country has plenty of gaps to address at home. Her argument was straightforward: build more colleges and hostels for Indian students first. But not everyone agreed. Several people responding to the post pointed out that government-funded scholarships for foreign students aren't necessarily random handouts. They can form part of bilateral relationships and international education programmes, where both countries offer opportunities to each other's students. One user described it as a âbilateral agreement between Tanzanian and Indian Governmentâ, calling such arrangements a fairly standard form of goodwill between countries. Another pointed out that student-exchange programmes operate across the world and asked whether the same criticism would apply to Indian students who receive scholarships or other support while studying abroad. The Erasmus Mundus scholarship was also brought into the discussion, with one commenter arguing that Indian students have benefited significantly from international scholarship programmes as well. Then came the question of exactly how the Tanzanian student was being funded. Some users claimed that the Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR), which facilitates several scholarship programmes for international students, provides stipends to cover living expenses while students are in India. One commenter put the figure at around â¹20,000 a month, although the exact amount and benefits can vary depending on the scholarship programme. Others argued that these initiatives aren't simply about education. Scholarships and student exchanges can also strengthen relationships between countries, creating goodwill and potentially supporting wider diplomatic, cultural and economic ties. And that's where the online debate has become interesting. One side sees a foreign student receiving money from the Indian government and asks a very simple question: Shouldn't Indian taxpayers come first? The other sees international education as part of how countries build relationships. Students who study in India return home with professional connections, familiarity with the country and, potentially, a more positive view of India. So, what started with a student talking about his stipend on Latent has turned into a much bigger argument about what taxpayer money should fund, how international scholarships work and whether spending on foreign students can actually serve India's interests in the long run. The bigger question isn't necessarily whether India should fund foreign students at all. title: Comedy can blend with other genres or stand on its own: Monika Shergill
text: Monika Shergill âEveryoneâs brand of humour is different, and we really want to have that diversity and quality in comedy,â says Monika Shergill, VP, Content, Netflix India. Ahead of the announcement of Netflixâs latest comedy slate, Har Type Ka Funny, she spoke to us about how the platform programs comedy and what she has learned about Indian audiences in the last decade. What distinguishes Indian viewers, she says, is their willingness to experiment. âI would say they are more experimental than most audiences around the world, because we are very open to different languages, and we are a culture that wants to experience other places and other languages. We are very curious people. We want to know, we want to find our place within the world,â Shergill says. That curiosity, she explains, coexists with a strong loyalty to homegrown stories. âWe are very loyal to our own content, but we also want to experiment and watch and learn from other peopleâs stories,â she says. What makes Indian viewers laugh? Itâs all about variety The slate moves across films, stand-up and family entertainment. It includes Chumbak, Season 5 of The Kapil Sharma Show and Indiaâs Got Latent, alongside new stand-up from Zakir Khan and Dhamaal 4. âWe are bringing Zakir Khanâs very beautiful special called Papa Yaar,â Shergill says. Writer-director Aatish Kapadia and producer J.D. Majethia - the pair behind Khichdi and Sarabhai vs Sarabhai are bringing Chumbak. âThey are bringing a neighbourhood comedy. Itâs got a great cast, a very, very big cast, and itâs in two batches - eight episodes and another batch of eight episodes.â The show marks a reunion between the two collaborators. Bhuvan Bam is set to return separately with Dhindora Season 2. Shergill says the platform has to program for different kinds of audiences. âWe have to program for different kinds of audiences. Even in rom-coms, if I were to take South comedies (such as Vishwanath & Sons) that weâve done, or the blockbuster films that we bring, like Dhamaal 4 right now, which has become such a big comedy film of the year. Itâs a great friends-watch-party kind of film, or a family getting together on a weekend and wanting to watch it. â âAnd then we have something like Maa Behen, which is delivered in comedy treatment, then we had Toaster. Comedy is something which can blend with other genres or stand on its own and bring you something completely unique, depending on the voice of the creator. For us, itâs creating a whole new range of creative voices on Netflix who bring their own brand of humour,â she says. âCreators of Chumbak found the found-family concept, and they created a delightful world around itâ The idea for Chumbak, Shergill says, grew out of something recognisable in Indian city life. âIn cities, everyoneâs families are in different places, and your neighbours are your family. So the creators of Chumbak found the found-family concept, and they created a delightful world around it,â she says. âTheir brand of comedy is really warm, sweet comedy. It is very accessible comedy.â With Zakir Khan, the draw was a distinct comic voice. âZakir is known to have a certain voice, a certain brand of humour. So, we wanted to bring Zakir on the service for a long time, and he had this special, which we thought was something that was totally unmissable,â Shergill says. âWe wanted to give every single flavour, and thatâs how we choseâ She describes the same thinking as guiding how the platform supports its other comedians. âItâs also a very deep responsibility that we take, that every creatorâs creative voice coming on Netflix should feel that their reach is widening, and their voice is reaching audiences across India and across the world,â she says, citing The Kapil Sharma Show as an example of a series that keeps growing season over season. âSunil (Grover), whoâs such a talented comedian, has had an absolute breakout season with Season 4. â For Shergill, it comes down to choice. âThe idea is to make each very unique, have different flavours, so their audiences have a choice, which is essentially the job of the streaming offering. And also to be able to satisfy many different types of audiences by making them go from one to the other,â she says. âComedy is also a genre where you can watch something alone. And then you can watch with friends or family. So, a community watch. I think we wanted to give every single flavour, and thatâs how we chose.â âPeople across the world are consuming content coming from different cultures, different languagesâ Indian comedy travels far within the Indian diaspora rather than across other-language markets. âWe have very wide viewing across India, also across the different countries where there is an Indian diaspora. I canât say that people from other nationalities and ethnicities or languages would be watching it in large numbers,â she says. She points to Netflixâs broader viewing patterns. âIâm sure on Netflix, we have 70% of our viewing across the world, in subs and dubs, of any content, whether itâs Hindi content travelling around the world, or itâs French, or Spanish, or Japanese content coming into India. 70% of all viewing on Netflix is in subtitles and dubs, which tells you that people across the world are consuming content coming from different cultures, different languages. â âBut comedy is more specific to the language context. So I would say more of the diaspora would be watching, and they are watching a lot because the audience is expanding for comedy,â she adds. Itâs a very good thing to have more experimentation and to have a higher bar for quality: Monika Shergill Whatâs her broader read on Indian audiences? She points to their appetite for content from elsewhere. âIndian audiences experiment. We watch a lot of K-dramas, we watch a lot of anime. Hollywood has always been big, as India has been a big market for inbound Hollywood content. Shows like Money Heist actually made a very big impact in India. Itâs one of the best-performing shows across Indian audiences, and also, even if you take a very niche show like Dark, which is a German show, Indian audiences watched it. India was one of the major audiences for Dark. â That openness, she argues, is also raising the bar for what audiences expect. âIf you look at what streaming has done, because it brings all this content, and particularly Netflix, from around the world, what happens is that as audiences watch more, they also evolve. Their tastes evolve, and they are looking for a certain kind of quality. They are looking for fresher stories.â âThat raises the bar for Indian creators. It raises the bar for us as executives, who have to work and program for a better and better slate, give more and better stories and options.â âItâs a good thing. Itâs a very good thing to have more experimentation and to have a higher bar for quality, because eventually it will mean only good things for our industry,â Shergill says. title: 'Kashmir pandit's pain not a punchline': J&K Peace Forum slams Samay Raina, Sharon Verma
text: Comedians Samay Raina and Sharon Verma (Image Credit: ANI) SRINAGAR: "Suffering and displacement of Kashmiri Pandits should not be turned into a joke", the Jammu and Kashmir Peace Forum has criticised comedians Samay Raina and Sharon Verma over their exchange on India's Got Latent, Season 2. In a statement on Saturday, forum chairman Satish Mahaldar said comedy could have freedom, but that freedom also came with responsibility. He said the controversy should not be used to create hostility between Kashmiri Pandits and Kashmiri Muslims, or between Kashmiris and Biharis. Watch âThey Will Catch Youâ: Samay Raina Gets Felicitated After Cyber Cell Case "We believe that comedy must have freedom, but freedom must also carry responsibility. Bihar is not an insult. Kashmir is not a punchline. And the displacement and suffering of Kashmiri Pandits cannot be reduced to a convenient joke, social-media clip or publicity moment." "For more than three decades, Kashmiri Pandits have lived with the consequences of displacement, separation from ancestral homes and the loss of a sense of belonging. Even Samay Raina has publicly spoken about his family's experience of displacement and the trauma associated with leaving Kashmir. "That is precisely why the present controversy deserves a mature response. We are not asking for censorship. We are asking for sensitivity," said Mahaldar. "We also reject attempts to turn this controversy into hostility between Kashmiri Pandits and Kashmiri Muslims, or between Kashmiris and Biharis. No entire community should be judged by the words of an individual. Kashmir's history is complicated and its future must be built on truth, reconciliation, justice and mutual dignity," he added further. What happened on India's Got Latent? The criticism came after Raina and Verma exchanged jokes about their respective backgrounds. Verma, who is from Bihar and Raina, a Kashmiri Pandit, were seen roasting each other over their places of origin. Raina took a dig at Verma's Bihari roots and stereotypes about migration for work. Verma responded with a joke about Raina's Kashmiri identity and "getting stoned". She also said she had "atleast left her state by choice." The exchange has since drawn criticism from several political leaders. Samajwadi Party MP Harendra Singh Malik also condemned the remarks and said comedians should be mindful of people's sentiments. title: YouTube on Ranveer Allahbadia video: After a thorough review, the video ...
text: YouTube has removed the controversial episode of ' India's Got Latent ' featuring podcaster Ranveer Allahbadia , following directives from the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. In a statement, a YouTube spokesperson said it reviews government removal requests when notified through the correct legal processes, and also reviews content for violations of its Community Guidelines. âAnd, where appropriate, we restrict or remove content in keeping with local laws and our Terms of Service after a thorough review. All of these requests are tracked and included in our Transparency Report,â the spokesperson added. It added that after a thorough review, the flagged video was blocked. The NHRC had previously instructed YouTube to take down the episode, citing violations of various legal provisions, including the Bhartiya Nyay Sanhita (BNS), the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, and the Information Technology (IT) Act. In response, YouTube stated that it reviews government removal requests when notified through the correct legal processes and also reviews content for violations of its Community Guidelines. The platform added that it restricts or removes content in accordance with local laws and its Terms of Service after a thorough review. Following the incident, Assam Police registered an FIR against Allahbadia and four other social media influencers for promoting obscenity and engaging in sexually explicit discussions on the show. The controversy has sparked widespread criticism from celebrities and public figures, leading to increased scrutiny of online content and its regulation. In the wake of the incident, singer B Praak canceled his appearance on Allahbadia's podcast, expressing disapproval of the remarks made on the show. Allahbadia has issued a public apology, acknowledging the inappropriateness of his comments and expressing regret for his lapse in judgment.

title: Manoj Bajpayee reacts to Samay Raina's 'India's Got Latent 2' Bihari joke row: 'We should learn to laugh at ourselves and still not be hurt and offended'
text: Manoj Bajpayee reacts to Samay Raina's 'India's Got Latent 2' Bihari joke row: 'We should learn to laugh at ourselves and still not be hurt and offended' Manoj Bajpayee has weighed in on the ongoing controversy surrounding comedian Samay Raina's show 'India's Got Latent 2', which sparked debate after a segment involving humour on immigrants. The actor shared his thoughts during promotions for his upcoming film 'Last Man in Tower'. Manoj Bajpayee on the Samay Raina Controversy When asked by IANS about the incident on the show, where Samay Raina engaged in banter with Sharon Verma, with the two mocking each other's roots, Manoj said he wasn't bothered as long as the intent was harmless. He told IANS, "If it is all in jest, I actually don't mind it. We should learn to laugh at ourselves and laugh together, laugh at each other and still not be hurt and offended. So, this is what we should learn. We should have humour about ourselves, but at the same time we should have respect, not only for ourselves but also for the person that you are sitting with and where that person comes from. It's very very important. If two people are very easy with each other, they always laugh at each other." Manoj Bajpayee recalls the stereotype he faced during his struggling days Manoj Bajpayee then recounted a personal experience from his early days in Delhi, when he was harshly told off by a bus driver. He said, "When I was in Delhi, I was 18, and I was trying to get into a bus from the front door because this was my first time. So, I didn't know the rules of the city. So, the driver looked at me and shouted, 'Aye Bihari board from the back gate'. So, he didn't know that I was from Bihar, but actually I'm from Bihar. So, for him, every person who was doing that kind of a foolish mistake was from Bihar. I didn't mind it because first, he was right that I was from Bihar. Second, I was not wrong because I was new to the city and I was completely unfamiliar. But when I made friends with people from different states, we used to laugh at each other." He added, "We never got offended or hurt. But yes, there is a problem if somebody coming from somewhere becomes a problem for you or becomes a problem for the community. Then there is a problem. Till then it's, we should be able to laugh at each other, laugh at ourselves. That's a sign of a very healthy society." title: India's Got Latent row: Five key takeaways from SC hearing in Ranveer Allahbadia case
text: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday pulled up influencer Ranveer Allahbadia over his controversial remarks during his appearance on ' India's Got Latent '. The Supreme Court was hearing the social media influence Ranveer Allahbadia's plea against multiple FIRs. He had sought consolidation of multiple FIRs filed against him in connection with his remarks on "India's got Latent'. Here are five key takeaways from the top court's observations during the hearing: 'If this is not obscenity, what is it?' The bench comprising Justices Surya Kant and N Kotiswar Singh expressed strong disapproval over Ranveer Allahabadia 's remarks, stating, "Just because somebody thinks he becomes so popular and can speak any kind of words, can take entire society for granted? Is there anyone on earth who will like this language? There is something very dirty in his mind which has been vomited." "In name of freedom of speech, no one has licence to speak whatever they want against norms of society. Words you have used will make daughters, sisters, parents and even society feel ashamed. If this is not obscenity, what is it? Why should we quash or club FIRs against you," it added. Poll How Do You Feel About the Responsibility of Content Creators on Social Media? Freedom Should Have Boundaries Accountability Is Important Interim protection granted The court granted interim relief to Ranveer Allahabadia after senior advocate Abhinav Chandrachud highlighted death threats to his client. The court permitted Allahbadia to seek police protection in Maharashtra and Assam. The court also said Allahbadia, who claimed that he and his family were receiving death threats could approach Maharashtra or Assam police for protection. Deposit passport However, the court directed Ranveer Allahabadia to deposit his passport with police in Maharashtra's Thane, and asked him to not leave the country without prior permission of the court. "He shall not leave India without court's prior nod," the top court said. No further FIRs The Supreme Court said no further FIR shall be registered against him on the basis of the episode aired on show India's Got Latent. "If any other FIR is lodged against influencer Ranveer Allahbadia over his comments, he shall not be arrested," SC said. Earlier, the Mumbai and Guwahati Police had said in a joint statement the Youtuber and podcaster Allahbadia was "continuously out of contact with the investigative agencies". He has been named in FIRs filed by Maharashtra Cyber Department, Guwahati Police, and Jaipur Police in the 'India's Got Latent' case, the police said. No more episodes The Supreme Court has directed Allahbadia and his fellow influencers to cease airing any additional episodes of the controversial YouTube show until further notice. The Cyber Cell is investigating the case registered against Ranveer Allahbadia and others after he triggered an uproar with his offensive remarks on the show 'India's Got Latent.' Samay Raina , who hosts the show, has expressed regret for the incident, clarifying that entertainment was his sole purpose. In a statement on his Instagram post, Raina said, "Everything that has been happening has been too much for me to handle. I have removed all India's Got Latent videos from my channel. My only objective was to make people laugh and have a good time. I will fully cooperate with all agencies to ensure their inquiries are concluded fairly. Thank you."

title: Samay Raina sparks fresh controversy with Bihar-Kashmir banter on 'India's Got Latent 2'; political leaders REACT: 'Just stick to comedy'
text: Samay Raina sparks fresh controversy with Bihar-Kashmir banter on 'India's Got Latent 2'; political leaders REACT: 'Just stick to comedy' Comedian Samay Raina is once again at the centre of a controversy after his banter with fellow comedian Sharon Verma on 'India's Got Latent 2' triggered widespread criticism. It drew sharp reactions from political leaders across party lines over jokes touching on regional and community sentiments. What happened on Samay Raina'a show In the recent episode, Sharon Verma, a former contestant from the show's first season, appeared as a panellist alongside Samay, Orry, Archana Puran Singh, and Nishant Suri. During the exchange, Raina took a dig at Verma's Bihari roots and stereotypes around migration for work. Verma responded by joking about his Kashmiri identity and "getting stoned", further quipping that she had "at least left her state by choice. " While the banter appeared to be mutual and light-hearted on screen, with both comedians seemingly enjoying the exchange, clips from the episode soon triggered strong reactions online and caught the attention of political leaders, reigniting the debate around insensitive humour. Watch âThey Will Catch Youâ: Samay Raina Gets Felicitated After Cyber Cell Case Shiv Sena (UBT) slams Samay Raina Speaking to ANI, Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Anand Dubey strongly criticised the comedian. He said, "Samay Raina is a comedian. His comedy routines often feature a great deal of obscenity. He has been involved in numerous controversies before; he has always been a controversial figure... But Samay Raina has just made another controversial statement. His recent altercation with another comedian, Sharon Verma, reveals a profound lack of understanding on their part. These people will stoop to any level just to make money. Samay Raina understands neither Bihar nor Jammu and Kashmir properly. Although he hails from Jammu and Kashmir, he shows no loyalty to that region, and certainly none to the people of Bihar... Just stick to comedy. Why drag specific castes, states, or religions into it?" Bihar minister calls remarks 'intolerable' Bihar Education Minister Mithilesh Tiwari also weighed in, telling media, "Any derogatory remark against any citizen of our country is intolerable; those who make such comments are essentially talking about tearing the nation apart. We envision an undivided India; for us, the king and the commoner are equal, and there should be no discrimination in the country based on caste or creed. This is the clear stance of the BJP. " Mixed reactions from other leaders Shiv Sena leader Sanjay Nirupam offered a more nuanced take, saying, "Samay Raina's show is a comedy show, and I believe humour should be taken as humour. I know the remark related to Bihar wasn't good, and the way the girl connected to Bihar gave a sharp retort in the context of Kashmir didn't sit well with me either... The atrocities committed against Kashmiri Pandits â she, in some way, commented on those atrocities, and Samay Raina, who is a Kashmiri Pandit, was clapping for it. That didn't sit well with me either... I felt like the injustice faced by Kashmiri Pandits was being mocked, but in the end, I forgive both those kids. It was humour, and it should be taken as a joke... There is no place for obscenity in society. If someone spreads obscenity in the name of humour, then certainly there should be a ban on them." Congress leader Harish Rawat added, "Humour is a divine art form that uplifts people, gladdens the heart, and lightens the burden of worries. However, when you misuse it to portray a caste, community, or region in a derogatory or mocking manner, it diminishes the value of humour itself. Samay Raina needs to understand this." AAP leader Sanjay Singh took a more forgiving stance, stating, "I think that if a comedian says something like this, their intention is to make people laugh. In that process, sometimes they make mistakes. But I think it is not right to turn it into an issue and target them. Instead, one should engage in dialogue with them and explain." BJP leaders demand stricter laws BJP MLA RS Pathania condemned the remarks strongly, saying, "India has a collective flow, a collective sentiment; India has a history, India has a tradition, and India has a golden future. Mischievous acts like this have previously led to fines for Samay Raina, but by tearing apart the guidelines set by law, the Constitution, and social ethics, he has made the remark again. We condemn it." PDP leader Syed Tajamul Islam stressed the need for sensitivity towards Kashmiri Pandits, saying, "The land of Jammu & Kashmir remains incomplete without (Kashmiri Pandits)... They did not leave their homes out of mere choice. The way these personalities are sometimes treated, there is no room for such conduct in either religion or humanity... We await their return, but wherever they are, they deserve great respect. " Congress leader Tariq Anwar remarked, "We are civilised citizens of India. People are born in different places. While speaking, one should keep in mind that no one's feelings are hurt." BJP leader Ram Kadam went further, calling for legal action against such content. He said, "We all respect any artist's talent, his art, but if under the guise of art, someone's faith, belief, or sentiments are hurt, it simply means that the artist is crossing certain boundaries to cause pain to people. Now this has become a trend. For publicity stunts, people start dragging in gods and goddesses or sentiments... It all ends with an apology. .. Now the time has come to enact a strict law against this... Then no one will have the courage to do such things. Enacting a strict law is the need of the hour, but until such a law is made, the public should ban such people on social media so that their minds come to their senses... Whether it's Samay Raina or anyone else under the guise of art, no one's sentiments can be hurt, and if someone is doing that, they cannot be forgiven." No response yet from Samay Raina or Sharon Verma As political and public reactions continue to mount, both Samay Raina and Sharon Verma are yet to issue a public statement addressing the criticism surrounding the episode. This is not the first time Raina's show has landed him in controversy, with the comedian having previously faced backlash and fines over content on his platform. title: âIâve genuinely forgotten who I am when Iâm not The Rebel Kidâ: Apoorva Makhija opens up about moving to New York to 'get away from constant pressure to stay relevant' and her plans beyond Bollywood
text: Apoorva Makhija opens up about moving to New York (Image Credits Instagram) Content creator and social media personality Apoorva Makhija, widely recognised online as The Rebel Kid, has swapped her usual chaos for a classroom in New York, enrolling in an MBA programme at NYU Stern. The plan, she says, in a recent interview, is to eventually head back to India and launch a direct-to-consumer brand of her own. The relocation arrives more than a year after she found herself at the centre of a massive controversy stemming from her appearance on Samay Raina's 'India's Got Latent', where an ill-judged joke about a contestant's mother triggered widespread backlash and several FIRs filed against her under the IT Act. Apoorva Makhija on having no regrets, despite the chaos Now 25 and most recently seen on 'Lock Upp' Season 2, Apoorva insists she isn't looking back with remorse. In a conversation with Hindustan Times, she explained, "I've apologised and taken accountability whenever I've been wrong. I don't regret any of my decisions. I genuinely think it's all part of the plot. I get to live this absolutely crazy life where almost everything I do gets an extreme reaction." She's candid, though, about the price her impulsive streak has extracted. "My impulsiveness has definitely come at a cost sometimes. But I don't think I would go back and erase any of it, because without those mistakes, I wouldn't be the person I am right now or be standing at this point in my life." She continues, "Every mistake I've made, every bad decision, every difficult situation has somehow led me to exactly where I am today, moving to New York, trying to figure out my purpose, searching for meaning, and asking myself what more I want to do with my life. " Apoorva Makhija on stepping away from the persona At the heart of her decision to leave is something far more personal than career strategy: a need to disconnect from the relentless machinery of staying online and relevant. "I'm moving to the US partly to get away from this constant pressure to stay relevant, reinvent yourself, figure out what you have to say next, and keep maintaining an online persona all the time. I think somewhere along the way, I've genuinely forgotten who I am when I'm not being The Rebel Kid. " The weight of public scrutiny, she admits, isn't always easy to carry. "It feels like a lot of responsibility, and sometimes it feels like no matter what I do, somebody is going to criticize it. But at the same time, that is also the beauty of my life." Apoorva Makhija's return to Bollywood Asked whether a return to Bollywood is on the cards, Apoorva, who made her acting debut with 'Nadaaniyan' (2025) and has since appeared in a handful of web shows, is unambiguous. "I see myself coming back to India, but no, I don't see myself building a career in Bollywood." Apoorva Makhija on filling in the gaps in her business know-how The MBA, Makhija explains, is meant to plug a very specific gap she felt in her entrepreneurial toolkit, "Over the last few years, I've sold products for different businesses through my content. But there was a huge part of building a business that I didn't understand well, like operations and supply chain, which determine whether a company survives." She wants to go beyond being just the face of a brand, aiming instead to understand "operations, supply chain, unit economics, margins, and all the less glamorous things that actually determine whether a company survives. " Apoorva Makhija's journey across reality TV and films Apoorva Makhija first drew national attention with her explosive run on 'India's Got Latent', before taking her larger-than-life persona to 'Lock Upp' Season 2. She also appeared on the reality show 'The Traitors', further cementing her reputation as one of the most talked-about faces of India's creator economy. title: All Indian Cine Workers Association calls for ban on 'India's Got Latent' over Ranveer Allahbadia's remarks on the show
text: The All Indian Cine Workers Association ( AICWA ) has strongly condemned YouTuber Ranveer Allahbadia 's remarks on the show ' India's Got Latent ,' hosted by comedian Samay Raina , and has demanded an "immediate ban" on the show along with legal action against those involved. In a press release shared on Monday evening, AICWA stated that Allahbadia's comments were offensive and went against "societal and family values." The association also urged the Indian film industry to "boycott" and "cease any collaboration with individuals" involved in the show. Poll Should Ranveer Allahbadia be held accountable for his controversy? No, it's overblown Yes, responsibility matters "The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) vehemently condemns the reprehensible and offensive remarks made on the YouTube show India's Got Latent, hosted by Samay Raina. In a recent episode, Ranveer Allahbadia, who participated in the show, unleashed abhorrent and vile statements that are deeply disrespectful to our societal and family values. Such disgraceful content is utterly unacceptable and poses a significant threat to the moral fabric of our society," AICWA wrote. "Representing the entire Indian film industry, AICWA officially boycotts India's Got Latent. We call upon all actors, filmmakers, directors, and technicians to immediately cease any collaboration with individuals involved in this show, including host Samay Raina and Ranveer Allahbadia. Henceforth, these individuals will receive no support from the Indian film industry," the statement further read. AICWA also added a list of demands, which included a complete ban on 'India's Got Latent,' strict legal action against Ranveer Allahbadia and Samay Raina, FIRs against all responsible individuals, and stronger regulations for digital content to prevent similar incidents, among others. The controversy began after Allahbadia aka BeerBiceps made a crass joke during an episode of 'India's Got Latent'. His comment quickly went viral, leading to widespread backlash from artists and social media users. During an appearance on the show, the podcaster asked a contestant, "Would you rather watch your parents... or join in once and stop it forever?" Allahbadia later apologized for his "inappropriate" remarks that were made in an "insensitive" manner during the YouTube episode of the show. He issued an apology in a video that he shared on his X account hours after facing backlash, saying that "comedy is not his forte" and that "it wasn't cool." Admitting that his comments were "inappropriate," the podcaster said, "My comment wasn't just inappropriate, it wasn't even funny. Comedy is not my forte, I am just here to say sorry." "Obviously, this is not how I wish to use it. I am not going to give any context, justification, or reasoning behind what happened. I am just here for an apology. I personally had a lapse in judgment. It wasn't cool on my part," he added. He also addressed concerns about his influence on younger audiences, saying, "The podcast is watched by people of all ages. I don't want to be the kind of person who takes that responsibility lightly. Family is the last thing that I would ever disrespect. I need to use this platform better. That has been my learning from this whole experience. I promise to get better," he said. Allahbadia added that he has asked India's Got Latent to remove "insensitive sections" from the episode that featured him. "I have asked the makers of the video to remove the insensitive sections from the video. All I can say in the end is sorry, I hope you can forgive me as a human being," he said. A complaint was filed with the Mumbai Commissioner and the Maharashtra Women's Commission in which the complainant alleged that the show used abusive language and made obscene remarks about women. The complaint states that the remarks were made to gain popularity and financial benefit through online broadcasts.

title: India's Got Latent row: Supreme Court directs return of Ranveer Allahbadia's passport
text: Ranveer Allahbadia NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday allowed podcaster Ranveer Allahbadia to reclaim his passport to travel abroad over work. A bench of Justices Surya Kant and N Kotiswar Singh relaxed the condition after Assam and Maharashtra governments said the investigation against the influencer in the "India's Got Latent" case was complete. The bench asked Allahbadia to approach the Maharashtra cyber police bureau for his passport, according to news agency PTI. The apex court also told senior advocate Abhinav Chandrachud, appearing for Allahbadia, that on the next hearing, it would consider Allahbadia's prayer for clubbing the FIRs registered against the YouTuber, and bring it in one place. On February 18, the Supreme Court protected Allahbadia from arrest in multiple FIRs filed over his comments during an episode of India's Got Latent. It also directed him to deposit his passport with the investigating officer of Police Station Nodal Cyber Police, Thane. Poll What impact do you think the 'India's Got Latent' case will have on future podcast content? Increased censorship More responsible content creation On March 3, he was allowed to resume his podcast "The Ranveer Show" subject to maintaining "morality and decency," and making it "suitable" for viewers of all ages. The apex court had initially restrained Allahbadia, popularly known as "BeerBiceps," from airing any programme of his podcast. This was done to avoid any "direct or indirect" bearing on the merits of the sub-judice cases he was involved in. On February 18, the top court granted interim protection from arrest to Allahbadia while calling his comments "vulgar" and saying he had "dirty mind" which "put the society to shame." Aside from Allahbadia and comedian Samay Raina, who created India's Got Latent, others named in the case in Assam are comics Ashish Chanchlani, Jaspreet Singh and Apoorva Makhija. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court bench also allowed Cure SMA Foundation, a Gururgam-based patients support association, to file a separate petition impleading Raina, social media influencers, and persons who have been "ridiculing" physical and other deficiencies in people to create bias in society towards them. title: India's Got Latent Row: Samay Raina appears before Guwahati Police for questioning
text: Comedian Samay Raina appeared before the Guwahati Crime Branch on Saturday in connection with the case filed against him for allegedly promoting obscenity and vulgar content through his YouTube show 'India's Got Latent. ' Comedian Samay Raina appeared before the Guwahati Crime Branch on Saturday in connection with the case filed against him for allegedly promoting obscenity and vulgar content through his YouTube show 'India's Got Latent. ' The alleged accused, Samay Raina, earlier informed the Guwahati Police that he wouldn't be able to appear before them as he was out of India for his comedy tour. On Saturday, Samay visited the Guwahati Crime Branch to record his statement by the investigating officer. While talking to ANI, Ankur Jain, Joint Police Commissioner, Guwahati, said that police questioned Samay Raina and recorded his statement in connection to the case. On February 10, Guwahati Police had registered an FIR against certain YouTubers and social Influencers, namely Ashish Chanchlani, Jaspreet Singh, Apoorva Makhija, Ranveer Allahbadia, Samay Raina and others for promoting obscenity and engaging in sexually explicit and vulgar discussion in a show titled "India's Got Latent". Guwahati Crime Branch had registered a case vide Cyber PS case no 03/2025 under sections - 79/95/294/296 of BNS 2023 read with Sec 67 of IT Act, 2000, read with Section 4/7 of Cinematograph Act 1952 read with Section 4/6 of Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986. Earlier, Youtuber Ashish Chanchlani, who is also one of the alleged accused in the case, along with influencer Apoorva Makhija, podcaster Ranveer Allahbadia, comedian Samay Raina and others, also appeared before the Guwahati Crime Branch to record his statement. In light of the ongoing legal issues, Raina recently made a decision to reschedule his India tour. He took to Instagram to share the news, assuring fans that refunds would be provided for tickets. "Hello guys, I am rescheduling my India tour. You all will get the refunds shortly, see you soon," he wrote. Joint Police Commissioner Ankur Jain confirmed that notices had been served to several individuals named in the FIR, including Raina, Chanchlani, Allahbadia, and others. "We have served notices, but they have not complied yet. We are looking into the matter as per legal procedure and will take action accordingly," Jain said. Similarly, Rakesh Sawant, who also appeared on India's Got Latent, was summoned by the Maharashtra Cyber Cell, appearing to record her statement on February 27. The show came under intense scrutiny after controversial remarks were made by Ranveer Allahbadia during a recent episode. Allahbadia's comment about a contestant involving their parents quickly went viral and was met with widespread criticism on social media. title: SC quashes all FIRs against Samay Raina, Ranveer Allahabadia in âIndiaâs Got Latentâ case
text: SC quashes all FIRs against Samay Raina, Ranveer Allahbadia NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday closed criminal proceedings against comedian Samay Raina and four other social media personalities over remarks concerning people with disabilities, while recognising their subsequent efforts to promote awareness and dignity for the community. Along with Raina, the court quashed the FIRs and related proceedings against comedians Vipul Goyal, Balraj Paramjeet Singh Ghai, Sonali Thakkar and Nishant Jagdish Tanwar. Watch 'Brazenly Violated Our Order': Supreme Court Imposes â¹3 Lakh Fine On Comedian Samay Raina The proceedings stemmed from jokes made by the five, which were flagged by the M/s SMA Cure Foundation, an organisation working with people affected by Spinal Muscular Atrophy and other rare diseases. The case took a different turn after the Supreme Court asked the influencers to take constructive steps towards supporting people with disabilities. The court noted that they had since organised a chess tournament for specially-abled people in March and helped raise awareness about organisations working with people with disabilities. The bench, comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said their efforts appeared to be producing positive results. "Once there are genuine efforts, positive results are bound to be there," the bench said as per news agency PTI. "They are very bright youngsters. If they have started working in the positive direction, they will bring positive results," it added. Senior advocate Aparajita Singh, appearing for the SMA Cure Foundation, told the court that the influencers had made "genuine efforts" and had attempted to engage with the foundation following the court's earlier intervention. "This matter was going nowhere till this court took a very strong stand last time," Singh said. The court subsequently quashed the FIRs and other criminal proceedings against the five and said their case was now closed. However, the Supreme Court said it would separately examine the larger question of how the dignity of people with disabilities can be better protected and whether comprehensive directions are required. The court's observations came a day after the CJI and other judges met a delegation of people with disabilities from different fields. "It was quite a learning and an eye-opener for us also," the CJI said, adding, "We have requested them to send their suggestions also." "It was quite a satisfying experience what we saw yesterday and what we interacted," he said. The delegation included 20 people, among them Paralympians and athletes such as Nidhi Mishra, Ankur Dhama and Major D P Singh, as well as Chhonzin Angmo. Officials confirmed that Raina has requested more time to respond to the summons as he is scheduled to return from US by third week of March. âMaa-Bahen Ki Izzatâ¦â Ranveer Allahbadiaâs âvulgarâ jokes at Samay Rainaâs show stirs row|FIR lodged Poll How Do You Feel About the Responsibility of Content Creators on Social Media? There Should Be Clearer Guidelines for Content Creators Should Be More Mindful of Their Words The State Cyber Cell has issued notices to approximately 40 individuals who participated in filming 18 episodes of India's Got Latent. Additionally, the Cyber Cell has requested YouTube to take down all 18 episodes from its platform. A Cyber Cell officer confirmed that YouTube had already removed the controversial episode within two days of its upload. "Though we can't see the episodes online, we are in touch with YouTube to remove the entire content. Meanwhile, it was learned that comedian Samay Raina removed the episode he had uploaded yesterday," the officer said. The officer also indicated that notices have been issued to all content creators, organizers, and attendees. "So far, no arrests have been made. Action will be initiated after recording statements and scrutinizing the content," the officer added. The Khar police have collected statements from at least 10 individuals following a written complaint about the matter, as the episodes were filmed at a studio in Khar in November 2024. Broke silence Breaking his silence on the matter, Raina on Wednesday took to Instagram to address the backlash. He announced that he has taken down all videos of India's Got Latent from his channel and assured full cooperation with authorities. "Everything that has been happening has been too much for me to handle. I have removed all India's Got Latent videos from my channel. My only objective was to make people laugh and have a good time. I will fully cooperate with all agencies to ensure their inquiries are concluded fairly. Thank you," Raina wrote. The controversy erupted after a remark made by YouTuber Ranveer Allahbadia in a recent episode triggered a backlash. A formal complaint was subsequently filed against Allahbadia, social media influencer Apoorva Makhija, Raina, and the organizers of India's Got Latent. Meanwhile, Allahbadia had earlier issued a public apology, admitting that his comments were "inappropriate" and that he "had a lapse in judgment." The investigation into the case remains ongoing. title: Complaint filed against YouTuber Ranveer Allahbadia, Apoorva Makhija, Samay Raina, and the organizers of the show 'India's Got Latent' over controversial comment
text: In a storm that has gripped Mumbaiâs media landscape, popular YouTuber and podcaster Ranveer Allahbadia, also known as "BeerBiceps," finds himself in hot water after a controversial comment during the latest episode of the show 'India's Got Latent. ' The remark, deemed vulgar and offensive by many, has triggered outrage across social media and led to an official complaint filed with the Mumbai Commissioner and Maharashtra Women's Commission. The letter submitted to the Mumbai Commissioner and Maharashtra Women's Commission demanded strict action for allegedly using abusive language on the show, reports ANI. The incident unfolded when Allahbadia posed an unsettling question to a contestant: âWould you rather watch your parents have sex every day for the rest of your life or join in once and stop it forever?â Poll How Do You Feel About the Responsibility of Content Creators on Social Media? Creators Should Be More Mindful of Their Words There Should Be Clearer Guidelines for Content The bizarre and inappropriate remark, made in the presence of co-panelists like social media influencer Apoorva Makhija, comedian Samay Raina, and content creator Ashish Chanchlani , went viral almost instantly. Clips circulated furiously across social media, drawing widespread criticism. See more: Ranveer Allahbadia Controversy Live Update: Famous YouTuber under radar after his India's Got Latent row Journalist and lyricist Neelesh Misra didnât mince words in his fiery response. Calling out what he labeled "perverted creators" shaping India's creative economy, Misra blasted the show and its creators in a scathing social media post: "This content is not designated as adult contentâit can be seen with ease even by a child if the algorithm takes him or her there. The creators of the platform have zero sense of responsibility. I am not surprised that four people at the deskâand lots in the audienceâcelebrated this and had a great laugh. Decency is not incentivized in Indiaâby platforms or audiencesâand creators are stooping lower and lower for audience reach and revenue." The post struck a chord with netizens, many of whom echoed Misraâs sentiments. The backlash swiftly transitioned from online outrage to legal action, with a formal complaint filed against Allahbadia, Apoorva Makhija, Samay Raina, and the showâs organizers. As of now, neither Allahbadia nor the show's producers have issued a statement. But the controversy raises critical questions: How far is too far in the quest for viral content? And at what cost is "entertainment" being redefined in the digital age? The controversy quickly entered political circles, with Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis stressing that "freedom has limits." Congress spokesperson Supriya Shrinate slammed the remark as "perverse," while digital creator Aashish Chandorkar called for higher ethical standards in digital content.Under mounting backlash, Ranveer Allahbadia issued a public apology, admitting to a "lapse in judgment" and promising to remove the insensitive content while improving his platform's curation. But in a surprising twist, a post on X revealed that Allahbadia's controversial question wasn't original. A resurfaced video showed comedians from the OG Crew making the exact same joke on a different YouTube show just two weeks earlier. The clip featured a woman named Sam and a man named Allen laughing over the remark, sparking debate over whether Allahbadia was unfairly targeted for recycling existing content.This revelation has reignited discussions about originality, accountability, and ethical boundaries in Indiaâs digital ecosystem. Was Allahbadia guilty of poor judgmentâor merely a casualty of borrowed controversy? The debate continues.

title: Samay Raina urges netizens to be kind to Sakshi Jha after India's Got Latent episode and not troll her: 'Waha par bhi ek insaan hai'
text: The third episode of Indiaâs Got Latent quickly became a talking point because of contestant Sakshi Jhaâs remarks during her performance. She described herself as a "man hater" and later said she was a "feminist. " In response, Raghu Ram told her not to identify as a feminist if she believed misandry represented feminism. Following the episodeâs release on YouTube and Netflix, Jha found herself facing intense backlash across social media. The Bihar-based teacher soon became the focus of memes on social media. Amidst that, Samay Raina has now appealed to viewers to show compassion towards Sakshi, after episode three triggered widespread criticism over her comments about men. Taking to social media, Raina acknowledged that Jha had become the target of countless memes but urged people not to let the trolling cross the line into personal attacks. He joked that he had packed his bags and headed to Alibag as soon as the episode was released, saying he knew another controversy was likely on its way. Watch Raghu Ram and wifey Natalie Di Luccio reveal their son Rhythm's picture for the first time with a heartfelt poem In one of his videos, Raina addressed the trolling directly. "Bahaut sare memes ban rhe hain 'man hater' Sakshi Jha ke ('Man hater' Sakshi Jha is the new subject of memes]." He followed it with an appeal: "But request hai mere 'mens' ke liye [I have a request for 'mens'), just be kind to her man." Explaining his perspective, Raina said Indiaâs Got Latent is a platform where contestants often say unexpected things and added that performing on its stage is far from easy. He admitted he was saddened by the amount of hate directed at Jha and asked viewers to ensure their criticism remained respectful. While he said he had no objection to light-hearted jokes, he reminded people, "But remember, waha par bhi ek insaan hai (Remember that there is a human being at the receiving end). " The comedian also encouraged his followers to support Jha, saying it was the perfect opportunity to send her kindness. "It will show her that 'mens' are amazing people, too," he remarked. Raina further credited Jha for making the latest episode memorable, saying that without her contribution, it would not have been as successful. "You have to give it to her," he added. In another Instagram Story, Raina tagged Jha and wrote, "Sending you lots of love from 'mens'." During her appearance on the show, Jha repeatedly referred to herself as a "man hater" and reacted with "chhee" (eww) while making a face whenever "mard" (men) were mentioned. She also claimed that she hated her father, grandfather and brother, saying she had even told her father this directly. When Vishal Dadlani questioned her about her stated fantasy of beating her husband, Jha clarified that she meant doing so after consuming alcohol. Defending the remark humorously, she said that as someone from Gen Z, "kuchh to alag hona chahiye na" (something should be different). Jha also described a "good man" as someone who unquestioningly obeys his wife, or a "joru ka gulaam." Her statements rapidly spread online, sparking debates about feminism and prompting many users to argue that the zero scores she received from every judge accurately reflected her performance on Indiaâs Got Latent 2. The second season of Indiaâs Got Latent marked Samay Rainaâs return after the controversy surrounding the previous season. Its opening episode, featuring actors Alia Bhatt and Sharvari Wagh, received mixed reactions, with some viewers welcoming the show's comeback while others felt it lacked the spontaneous, unfiltered charm that had previously made it a viral sensation. title: SC slams YouTuber Ranveer Allahbadia but shields him from arrest, seeks help to regulate social media content
text: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday condemned influencer Ranveer Allahbadia for his offensive remarks on the âIndia's Got Latent ' show but shielded him against arrest in FIRs lodged in various states. The court sought assistance of top law officers to "devise something" to stop "anything and everything" from being broadcast on social media under the guise of free speech. A bench of Justices Surya Kant and N Kotiswar Singh gave Allahbadia interim protection from arrest in connection with FIRs registered at Thane, Guwahati and Jaipur but restrained him and his associates from airing any show till further orders. The YouTuber had made the offensive remarks as one of the panelists in comedian Samay Raina's show, which was launched last June. The bench said, "There is complete lack of responsibility and the behaviour is condemnable. He thinks he is popular and can say anything taking the entire society for granted and get away with it. Would anyone...like the kind of words he used? There is something very dirty in his mind that has been vomited out in this programme." As Allahbadia's counsel said the petitioner was getting life threats, the bench told him to approach local police for protection but asked him not to take his lawyers along while joining the investigations. SC ordered him to deposit his passport with the investigating officer at Thane and barred him from travelling abroad without the apex court's prior permission. Alarmed by the deteriorating standards of language and content in certain programmes broadcast on social media, the bench sought the assistance of attorney general R Venkataramani and solicitor general Tushar Mehta during the next hearing in "devising something" to regulate "anything and everything" being aired on certain websites and online channels in the name of right to freedom of speech and expression. As Abhinav Chandrachud defended the controversial remark by attempting to differentiate it from vulgarity or obscenity, Justices Kant and Singh asked, "If this (the remark) is not obscenity, then what is that standard or parameter of obscenity? Do you have a licence to speak all kinds of vulgarity and exhibit your depraved mind anywhere and at any time?" Citing SC rulings in Arnab Goswami, Amish Devgan and Apoorva Arora cases, Chandrachud sought clubbing of the FIRs at one place and said Allahbadia's statement is not so grave as to invite criminal prosecution. He said SC has explained what is obscenity in the Apoorva Arora case and had said anything that invites disgust and revulsion may not necessarily invite criminal prosecution. Profanity is not obscenity, he said. Justice Kant asked, "Does Apoorva judgment give you the licence to utter all kinds of nonsense? Look at the depraved and disgusting language you are using. The words you have chosen will put to shame every parent, daughters, sisters as well as brothers and society as a whole. Everyone will feel ashamed by the perverted mind you and your henchmen have exhibited." On Allahbadia being threatened on social media platforms, the bench said, "If someone commits a wrong, he would be dealt with by law. People cannot decide who is right or wrong and punish a person by taking law into their own hands. We strongly disapprove of such extension of threats to Allahbadia. But there is no actual threat to your life. As there are only three FIRs, you go and defend yourself." "Only because a litigant can afford to approach the highest court straightaway, can he demand that he does not want to go to so many places and that the investigations should be carried out at a place of his choice? If he is getting threats, the state will extend requisite protection to him," it said. The bench said the Guwahati FIR is very different from the Thane FIR as the former is more comprehensive and also refers to "dirty, humiliating and insulting language used against the residents of Arunachal Pradesh. There are different ingredients mentioned in the two FIRs." In a lighter vein, it said, "If you can try to get cheap publicity by using abusive language, then someone would try to get cheap popularity by threatening on social media. Every day, it happens." Chandrachud said the petitioner's mother is a doctor and that her patients are abusing her at the clinic. The bench said, "He should be ashamed of the mess he has created for himself and pain he has caused to his parents. We know from where he has copied. We know how he has copied from an Australian programme and which actor's dialogue he has stolen. But these foreign programmes contain all kinds of precautions. But you do not care about putting out those precautions for the public." Stay updated with breaking news , weather updates, bank holidays and upcoming public holidays in march .

title: India's Got Latent row: Samay Raina gets second summons from Maharashtra cyber cell
text: NEW DELHI: The Maharashtra Cyber Cell has issued a second summons to comedian and YouTuber Samay Raina , directing him to appear on March 19 to record his statement in connection with the Indiaâs Got Latent show. Raina was initially summoned today but did not appear before the Cyber Cell. He had previously requested to give his statement via videoconferencing from the United States, citing prior commitments preventing his return to India before March 17. The Cyber Cell rejected his request, maintaining that his statement must be recorded in person. The controversy erupted after Allahbadia asked a contestant: "Would you rather watch your parents... or join in once and stop it forever?" Raina responded to the backlash on Instagram, stating: "Everything that has been happening has been too much for me to handle. I have removed all India's Got Latent videos from my channel. My only objective was to make people laugh and have a good time. I will fully cooperate with all agencies to ensure their inquiries are concluded fairly." Multiple FIRs were filed in Maharashtra and Assam against the involved parties. Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma confirmed that Guwahati Police registered an FIR against Allahbadia, Raina, and others for promoting obscenity. The Supreme Court Justices Surya Kant and N Kotiswar Singh described Allahbadia's comments as "dirty and perverted," emphasizing that such behavior must be condemned. Allahbadia approached the Supreme Court to consolidate the charges against him. The Court granted him interim protection from arrest, conditional upon his cooperation with investigations. The Court imposed strict conditions, including surrendering his passport and requiring permission to leave the country. Justice Kant addressed the government regarding inappropriate content on platforms like YouTube, stating: "We would like you to do something. Otherwise, we are not going to leave this vacuum and barren area the way it is being misused." The Maharashtra Women's Commission supported the Supreme Court's intervention in stopping the controversial shows. The Commission's Chairperson Rupali Chakankar endorsed the Court's decision. The Commission had previously requested the Mumbai Commissioner to investigate the incident. The controversy also led to formal complaints against comedian Apoorva Makhija and the show's organizers, alongside Allahbadia and Raina.
